summary: This standards-track RFC defines new Certificate Signing Request attributes for Enrollment over Secure Transport. They disambiguate the overloaded uses of the challengePassword attribute from RFC 2985, such as revocation passwords, authentication passwords and EST uses.

eli5.summary: One field was used for several different purposes, causing confusion. This gives each purpose its own clearly named field.

questions: how does est use csr attributes
subtitle: Gives one-time passwords, revocation passwords and EST identity linking their own certificate request attributes.

tldr.problem: The PKCS #9 challengePassword attribute in a Certificate Signing Request has been overloaded: it can mean a revocation password, a one-time authentication password, or the EST link to the secure transport, and context alone says which.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7894 defines three new attributes, otpChallenge, revocationChallenge and estIdentityLinking, each with its own object identifier, so each meaning is stated explicitly.
tldr.outcome: EST servers can ask for any mix of these in a CSR Attributes Response, and clients must include each one they have a value for. The attributes supplement existing EST mechanisms and do not replace them.

today: RFC 7894 is a Proposed Standard from June 2016. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Overloaded Challenge Password
sections.content:
PKCS #9 (RFC 2985) defined a challengePassword attribute for Certificate Signing Requests (CSRs) as "a password by which an entity may request certificate revocation". Tooling parses and embeds it well, so many workflows reused it as a one-time password for authentication. The RFC points to many Simple Certificate Enrollment Protocol (SCEP) implementations as an example.

Enrollment over Secure Transport (EST, RFC 7030) added yet another meaning in its Section 3.5: linking the CSR to the secure transport. When only one use was needed at a time, the overloading caused no trouble. Implementation experience with EST showed that it is a limit when several uses are wanted separately or together.

The RFC gives an example: a server might require client authentication with an existing X.509 certificate, a username and password, a one-time password inside the CSR, and identity linking, all at once.
sections.eli5: Imagine one line on a form that sometimes asks for a secret word, sometimes a code, and sometimes a ticket number. You could not use two of those at the same time. This RFC fixes that.

sections.title: Three New Attributes
sections.content:
The RFC defines three attributes, each identified by its own object identifier (OID) under id-smime:

  • otpChallenge (id-aa-otpChallenge, 56) carries a one-time password inside a CSR.
  • revocationChallenge (id-aa-revocationChallenge, 57) states unambiguously the original PKCS #9 intent, a password for requesting revocation.
  • estIdentityLinking (id-aa-estIdentityLinking, 58) carries the EST link between the authenticated TLS session and the proof-of-possession in the request, with the semantics of Section 3.5 of RFC 7030.

The RFC says that generation, verification and storage of the one-time password value are not addressed. RFC 4226 and RFC 6238 define one-time password mechanisms that MAY be used.
sections.eli5: Instead of one overworked box there are now three: one for a one-time code, one for the cancel-my-certificate password, and one for proving you are the same person who logged in.

sections.title: Value Syntax and Encoding
sections.content:
Each attribute is a DirectoryString with a maximum length of 255, consistent with the original challengePassword. Reusing that shape lets implementations attach the new OIDs to their existing challengePassword parsing and generation code. In the ASN.1 module each attribute allows a single value (COUNTS MIN 1 MAX 1).

Generated values SHOULD use PrintableString whenever possible. If internationalization makes that impossible, UTF8String SHOULD be used. Systems that process the attributes MUST recognize and process both, and support for other string types is OPTIONAL.
sections.eli5: The new boxes hold short text, up to 255 characters, just like the old one. Plain letters and numbers are preferred, and fancier characters are allowed when needed.

sections.title: Indicating and Processing the Attributes
sections.content:
The EST server MUST indicate these attributes, as the use case requires, in every CSR Attributes Response. The client MUST include every indicated attribute for which it has values in the next CSR.

For legacy compatibility, a server MAY send both estIdentityLinking and challengePassword in a response. A client that sees estIdentityLinking SHOULD prefer it and not include challengePassword. A client that sends an unsolicited estIdentityLinking MAY also include challengePassword to support legacy servers.

The server MUST evaluate each challenge attribute independently, and all included challenge attributes MUST be processed successfully for the request to be valid. It MAY ignore attributes under local policy, for example estIdentityLinking when the client is an authenticated Registration Authority, and it MAY refuse requests not encoded according to the policy of the Certification Authority.
sections.eli5: The server tells the client which boxes to fill in. The client fills in every box it has an answer for, and the server checks each answer by itself. Every answer has to pass.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Beyond the considerations in RFC 7030, extra concerns depend on how the otpChallenge value is generated and verified. Where a one-time password is used, the security considerations of HOTP (RFC 4226) or TOTP (RFC 6238) may be relevant, and so are those from RFC 2985 that apply to the challenge attribute.

The introduction adds that carrying the authentication value as an attribute may be preferable to an HTTP or TLS password where the certificate request processing is separate from the HTTP/TLS termination point, for example behind a web application firewall.
sections.eli5: How safe the one-time code is depends on how it is made and checked, so the rules of those other code systems still apply.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The three attributes got object identifiers in the "SMI Security for S/MIME Attributes (1.2.840.113549.1.9.16.2)" registry: 56 for id-aa-otpChallenge, 57 for id-aa-revocationChallenge and 58 for id-aa-estIdentityLinking. Appendix A holds the ASN.1 module, id-mod-EST-Alt-Challenge, registered as value 87 in the "SMI Security for PKIX Module Identifier" registry.
sections.eli5: The official numbering office wrote the three new boxes into its list, each with its own number.
